The Level Ride

Self‑test

A shape has constant width if the distance between its two parallel supporting lines is the same in every direction. A circle is one. So is a Reuleaux polygon — arcs each centred on the opposite vertex — even though it has corners and no fixed centre. Lay a flat plank across the top and the gap to the floor is exactly that width: constant, so the plank rides level while the shape bobs beneath. The plank height is read straight from the support function — never from the contact point — so there is no tick at the corner-pivot. An ellipse is round and smooth but its width swings from 2b to 2a: spin it and the plank bobs. A circle (a=b) is the level limit — proving the signature is width, not roundness.
The Midway · the amusements district

Slide a flat plank across the top of this tumbling shape. It glides dead level — a marble set on it would never roll. And yet the shape underneath has no fixed centre: watch it bob and lurch as it rolls. Roundness is a red herring; a still centre is a red herring. The one secret is width — across any direction the shape never changes how wide it is, so the gap between floor and plank can never change either. This corner-cornered triangle holds the plank as flat as a circle would.

What you are watching

A shape has constant width if, no matter how you turn it, the distance between the two parallel lines that just kiss it on opposite sides is always the same. A circle obviously qualifies. The surprise is that it is not the only one. A Reuleaux triangle is built from three circular arcs, each one centred on the opposite corner and swept at the same radius w — the faint compass arcs on the shape draw exactly that construction. It has sharp corners and wanders all over the place as it rolls, yet across every direction it is exactly as wide. So the plank resting on its top — whose height above the floor is that width — never moves. Roll the shape and the plank glides dead level while the centroid beneath it visibly bobs and lurches. That gap, level plank over a wandering centre, is the whole exhibit.

The plank height is read straight from the support function — the closed-form distance to the supporting line in each direction — not from where the shape touches the floor. That matters: the contact point jumps from an arc to a corner and back as the shape rolls, and a renderer that derived the height from the contact would put a little tick at every corner-pivot. Reading the support height instead gives a number that is smooth right through the cusp — there is no discontinuity to hide. The trace pen on the right draws that height against the roll angle: for the Reuleaux it is a flat line, the most boring graph in the manor, and that flatness is the point.

Two more facts come for free. Every constant-width shape of width w has perimeter exactly π·w — Barbier's theorem — the circle's πd is just one case; the brass plate on the rail confirms it to a part in a trillion for every Reuleaux preset. And the break-the-width slider perturbs one arc's radius: drag it out and the shape is no longer constant width, the live Δwidth readout climbs off zero, and the plank starts to bob. The readout is honest — it is the real max−min of the plank height, and it grows smoothly with the break.

The neg-control — round didn't save it

Switch to the ellipse. It is round and perfectly smooth — no corners at all — and our intuition screams that this one should ride level. It does not. An ellipse is wider across its long axis (2a) than its short (2b), so as it turns the plank rises and falls into a periodic wave, two bobs per full turn. (We spin the ellipse rather than rolling it, because an ellipse does not roll level — spinning shows the width swing cleanly, apples-to-apples with the Reuleaux's roll.) The gap the plank rises and falls is exactly 2(a−b). Now squeeze the ellipse back toward a circle (a=b) and the wave flattens to nothing — the level limit. That is the proof the signature is constant width, not roundness or smoothness: a cornered triangle rides level, a smooth ellipse bobs, and only the circle is on both lists.

Honesty

EXACT, machine-precision claims are made for only two things, and only on the canonical Reuleaux presets (orders 3, 5, 7 at width w): (1) the support height is the same in every direction to <1e-12 (the closed-form support function reaches ~2.2e-16; sampling the boundary instead caps near 1e-9 — the trap we avoid), and (2) the perimeter equals π·w exactly (Barbier). The ellipse and the broken morph are labeled inequalities — their Δwidth is asserted only to be greater than a threshold, never claimed exact. The ellipse perimeter shown is a labeled Ramanujan approximation, not asserted. The roll animation, the compass-arc guides, and the wandering centroid are rendering and enter no tested number; the plank height, the widths, and the perimeter are all exact core values.

On the Midway's rolling run. This ride is kin to the estate's other pieces of physics you can watch tumble: The Top That Won't Fall (a flicked wheel that orbits the rope instead of falling), The Brazil-Nut Box (a buried bead that climbs when you shake the box), and the geometry rides The Banked Curve and The Brachistochrone. There a spin, a shake, a slope decides the motion; here a single number — the width — decides whether the ride is level.
